claim: Claims to be at risk of harm from his creditor if returned to Vietnam and seeks non-refoulement protection
requested_remedy: Claims to be at risk of harm from his creditor if returned to Vietnam and seeks non-refoulement protection

facts.F1: The Applicant first entered Hong Kong illegally in August 1989 under a false identity and was arrested, convicted, and sentenced to prison in 1995.
facts.F2: He was repatriated to Vietnam in February 1997.
facts.F3: Between 2000 and 2007, he repeatedly sneaked into Hong Kong on at least four occasions, was arrested, convicted, and sentenced to prison, before being repatriated to Vietnam.
facts.F4: In 2008, he settled in his home district in Vietnam and worked as a truck driver.
facts.F5: In 2013, he started his own delivery business and purchased a goods van with a loan from a local money lender.
facts.F6: By 2015, his business began to struggle, and he had difficulty making monthly interest payments to his creditor.
facts.F7: In August 2015, he sold his van and house to pay off most of the loan, but his creditor demanded payment of the remaining balance.
facts.F8: Fearing further threats from his creditor, the Applicant left Vietnam on 22 August 2015 for China and then sneaked into Hong Kong.
facts.F9: He raised a non-refoulement claim on 25 August 2015 and was released on recognizance pending the determination of his claim.
facts.F10: The Applicant completed a Non-refoulement Claim Form on 25 June 2016 and attended a screening interview with the Immigration Department with legal representation.
facts.F11: The Director of Immigration rejected the Applicant's claim on all applicable grounds in a Notice of Decision dated 7 November 2016.
facts.F12: The Applicant did not lodge an appeal to the Torture Claims Appeal Board, but instead filed an application for judicial review in February 2018.
facts.F13: The Applicant informed the Immigration Department that as of November 2019, he filed his appeal, acknowledged receiving a confirmation that the appeal was received.
facts.F14: The Applicant's appeal to the Board was eventually lodged on 8 October 2019 and dismissed on 23 June 2021, confirming the Director's decision.
facts.F15: The Applicant's creditor made demands of payment, but there is no evidence of official involvement or state actor involvement in the loan transactions between the Applicant and his money lender
facts.F16: Thus the Applicant is not able to satisfy the high threshold to establish persecutory harm inflicted by the state or persons or entities which the state is unwilling or unable to control.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the Director of Immigration's decision to reject the Applicant's non-refoulement claim was reasonable
Whether the Torture Claims Appeal Board's decision to dismiss the Applicant's appeal was reasonable
Whether the Applicant has established a reasonably arguable basis for judicial review

claim: The defendant pleaded guilty to 2 charges of Evasion of liability and one charge of Fraud
requested_remedy: The defendant pleaded guilty to 2 charges of Evasion of liability and one charge of Fraud

facts.F1: The defendant joined a Fung Shing Steel company as a clerk in June 2009 and resigned in October 2010.
facts.F2: The defendant repeatedly contacted a Ms Fung Po-yi who joined the company at around the same time, seeking to borrow some money from Ms Fung after her resignation.
facts.F3: The defendant claimed that she needed money for her divorce proceedings with her husband who owned a sportswear company.
facts.F4: Ms Fung started to lend money to the defendant since November 2010 by way of online or inter-bank transfers and ATM deposits.
facts.F5: As at 12th September 2011, the defendant had on 17 occasions borrowed a total sum of $33,253 from Ms Fung.
facts.F6: The defendant telephoned Ms Fung and told her that she had deposited a check in the amount of $100,000 into Ms Fung’s Bank of China account as repayment of the money borrowed, plus interests.
facts.F7: A check drawn from an account with Bank of China 012-831-00040424 was in fact deposited into Ms Fung’s account but had bounced.
facts.F8: Subsequent investigation revealed that the account had already been closed by the bank on 13th January 2010 due to returned cheques and overdraft of bank charges.
facts.F9: Despite the bounced check, Ms Fung continued to lend money to the defendant.
facts.F10: As at 9th March 2012, the defendant had on 39 different occasions borrowed a total of $87,953 from Ms Fung.
facts.F11: The defendant contacted Ms Fung again and said that another check of $500,000 had been deposited into Ms Fung’s account, being payment for the money owed together with interests and compensation for her loss from the late repayment.
facts.F12: Just like the first check, this check was also issued from the said Bank of China 012-831-00040424 account and bounced.
facts.F13: From 28th November 2010 to 17th September 2012, the defendant had borrowed a total of $203,253 from Ms Fung on 73 different occasions.
facts.F14: Sometime after 17th September 2012, the defendant proposed a new repayment plan.
facts.F15: The defendant claimed, falsely, that she would receive a substantial amount of funds of up to $10,000,000 from her divorce proceedings, but that the funds were being frozen in an HSBC account because she and her husband were being investigated by the Independent Commission Against Corruption.
facts.F16: The defendant claimed that only a third person could assist in retrieving the money from the frozen account.
facts.F17: The defendant promised to pay Ms Fung extra money if she was willing to help her out.
facts.F18: The defendant told Ms Fung that the staff of HSBC will be contacting her soon.
facts.F19: A certain Fiona Chu contacted Ms Fung via an online chat service, MSN, claiming to be a staff of HSBC.
facts.F20: Fiona Chu said that in order for Ms Fung to be able to access the money in the frozen account, Ms Fung would have to settle the administrative fees first.
facts.F21: Ms Fung was then instructed to deposit the administrative fees and guarantee money into the defendant’s bank account with Bank of China.
facts.F22: Ms Fung followed the instructions each time and made the various deposits but was told on every occasion that she had missed the payment deadline and so was not able to access the money in the frozen account.
facts.F23: Ms Fung contacted the defendant about the matter and the defendant told her that a lawyer Mr Cheung will contact Ms Fung to sort the matter out.
facts.F24: In late-November 2012, a person claiming to be Mr Cheung started to contact Ms Fung through another online chat service, LINE.
facts.F25: Mr Cheung told Ms Fung that she had to settle her own insurance charge and administrative fees before Ms Fung could retrieve the money in the frozen account.
facts.F26: Up to around March 2013, Ms Fung, as directed by the said Mr Cheung, had deposited around $344,250 into the defendant’s Bank of China account.
facts.F27: A person claiming to be Peggy Chau contacted Ms Fung via WhatsApp.
facts.F28: She said she was responsible for the defendant’s account with HSBC and reminded Ms Fung to continue to deposit the administrative fees.
facts.F29: In June 2013, a person Rachel Tsang claimed to be Peggy Chau’s supervisor contacted Ms Fung.
facts.F30: She told Ms Fung that the balance of the defendant’s account stood at $20,000,000 but that it was still frozen.
facts.F31: Ms Fung needed to continue to pay the administrative fees.
facts.F32: From April to October 2013, Ms Fung had transferred a total of around $800,000 into the defendant’s Bank of China account.
facts.F33: Up to November 2013, Ms Fung had made 200 deposits into the defendant’s Bank of China account.
facts.F34: Ms Fung had asked her husband and her daughter to make some of the deposits for her.
facts.F35: By that stage, Ms Fung had to seek financial assistance from them.
facts.F36: A total of $1,243,434 was deposited into the defendant’s said Bank of China account.
facts.F37: In mid-January 2014, Ms Fung tried to borrow money from relatives in order to settle the administrative fees.
facts.F38: Ms Fung felt suspicious and reported the matter to the Police.
facts.F39: The defendant was arrested on 29th January 2014.
facts.F40: The defendant confessed in the subsequent video recorded interviews that she had invented the characters of bank staff and lawyer to trick Ms Fung into depositing the money into the defendant’s Bank of China account.
facts.F41: The defendant claimed she acted alone, posing as Fiona Chu, Peggy Chau, Rachel Tsang and lawyer Mr Chueng.
facts.F42: She had used up all the money she had gotten from Ms Fung.
facts.F43: The defendant is of previously clear record.
facts.F44: A background report was prepared on the defendant.
facts.F47: According to the defendant’s mother and elder sister, the defendant’s father is an avid gambler who frequents local mah-jong parlours and Macau casinos.
facts.F48: The gambling has always been a source of financial and emotional stress for the family ever since the defendant was a child.
facts.F49: The defendant’s parents are divorced but they still live under the same roof so that they can look after the father during his prolonged period of cancer treatment.
facts.F50: Ms Fung suffered anxiety over the incessant demands from the defendant posing as the different characters for her to pay out more and more money.
facts.F51: By the end, Ms Fung had run out of funds and had to resort to her husband and daughter as well as relatives for help.
facts.F52: The defendant’s actions added to Ms Fung’s anxiety because now those closest and dearest to her were also involved.
facts.F53: Ms Fung is now left with the problem of repaying her friends and relatives from whom she had borrowed.
facts.F54: The defendant exploited Ms Fung's compassionate and trusting nature.
facts.F55: The defendant planned her fraud and it was executed with some sophistication, with the defendant using three different social media communication applications to avoid revealing her true identity when posing as the four different characters.

facts.F1: The Liquidators of 7 companies applied for leave to enter a funding arrangement to pursue a claim.
facts.F2: The vast majority of the Companies’ debt is held by bond holders, and it is unrealistic to approach them individually to fund the prospective claim.
facts.F3: The proposed funding agreement is with a Cayman incorporated closed end fund, whose investors are largely financial institutions.
facts.F4: The funder’s only interest in the proposed proceedings would be that arising under the funding agreement.
facts.F5: The funder would distribute the profits to its investors if the proceedings prove to be successful.
facts.F6: The court had previously held that the assignment of a cause of action by liquidators pursuant to a funding agreement to Remedy Asia Limited did not infringe the rules against maintenance and champerty.
facts.F7: The Court of Final Appeal had considered the current law of maintenance and champerty in Hong Kong in Unruh v Seeberger.
facts.F8: Ribeiro PJ explained the development of the law of maintenance and champerty and identified four categories of considerations which inform an assessment of whether or not an arrangement is objectionable on the grounds of maintenance and champerty.
facts.F9: The court considered the risks associated with allowing a funder with no interest in litigation to finance it, including the commoditisation of litigation and the encouragement of it to be viewed as a commercial venture rather than the enforcement of legal rights.
facts.F10: The court considered the risk of the funder being able to pressure the Liquidators or the lawyers to conduct the litigation improperly.
facts.F11: The court weighed the considerations and assessed whether in the individual case the risks were substantially controlled and there were countervailing public policy considerations, which justify permitting the arrangement.

reference_issues: Whether the commercial character of the funder effects an assessment of whether or not the proposed funding agreement infringes the common law rules against maintenance and champerty.
Whether the proposed funding agreement is in the interests of creditors and that it is in satisfactory terms.
